content.thinking:
I'm checking that the eye decal sizing projects correctly onto the sphere, making sure the 0.62-sized decal fits within the 0.8 diameter eyeball without clipping near the edges, and confirming the decal only applies to the eyeball part itself.

The iris at 94% coverage looks too distorted and oversized, giving a big-eye effect with just a thin dark rim—I'll scale it down to 0.5 instead. Now I'm setting the eye orientation direction to look sideways-forward with default world up, verifying the glow decal works, deciding to skip gill/vent decals in favor of a painted chevron on the mantle chest, and confirming unused ring/card properties don't need handling since droplets and sprays cover that visual need.

I'm now tallying up the total part count across all components—water, spikes, head, eyes, beak, mantle, ribs, blades, fins, glow strips, and arms with their sweeps, cuffs, cups, and beads—to estimate the overall detail budget.

That brings the total to roughly 280 parts, which should keep triangle counts manageable. I considered adding orange glow slit vents on the head sides, but after checking the geometry, the head and mantle surfaces overlap too much at that position and would conflict with the eye placement, so I'm scrapping the head vents idea and instead looking at putting an armor vent decal lower on the mantle flank—though that area turns out to be covered by the head's extended reach anyway.

Instead I'll add bioluminescent orange dot accents as dashed lines along the dorsal ridge of the arms, reusing the same paint function. For the head plating, I'm reworking the brow ridges to arc around the eye rims using a geometric frame centered on each eye, sweeping points through an angular range to form a curved brow shape rather than relying on elevation hits.

Writing brow sweep geometry...

I'm also adding a torus-shaped bezel ring encircling each eye, offset slightly along the eye direction and finished in gunmetal.

Now I'm attaching the eye geometry to proper joints—naming them eyeL and eyeR with explicit bone references—and defining the two gunmetal color variants. I'm also planning a small glowing orange sphere at the mantle tip to cap it off.

I'm adding a glow sphere at the tentacle tip as a light lure, then turning to how splash effects relate to the arms touching the water. I'm tallying up the full joint count across base, core, mantle, head, eyes, fins, arms, and feeding tentacles to make sure the skeleton totals 84 joints, and sketching how the core and mantle chain connect at the same starting position.

Restructuring the hierarchy: base is root, core becomes its child with an upward aim as the spine joint, and mantle, arms, and head all parent to core so bending propagates naturally. Tentacle chains get a "tentacle" role, and I'm noting the Catmull-Rom path just needs a points array of coordinate tuples, with the water base bone sitting at the origin.

For the lathe geometry, I'm defaulting the bone binding to whichever joint is closest to the given position, which resolves to base rather than core, but I'll specify it explicitly anyway. Droplets get merged into one geometry with matching position/normal/uv attributes and bound to base, and spikes are faceted cones aimed along a direction vector.

Writing the mantle sweep code...

Now I'm working out the bulb geometry at the base cap and confirming the point-cap taper at the tip works without needing a separate surface-based approach. For the fins, I'm sketching an outline profile in local u/v coordinates that attaches partway along the mantle's surface, trying to get the curve of points to form a convincing fin shape.

Checking that the outline forms a valid simple polygon without edges crossing when I apply corner smoothing, then setting a tapered thickness profile for the leaf-like fin and thinking about how to tilt its plane relative to the mantle's local axes.

Writing fin paint function for radial rays...

Still tuning fin colors and edge shading...

Extending the orange rim highlight to the blade tips for consistent accenting, then I'm working out the overall bounding box dimensions by tracing the arm angles and lateral offsets to find the maximum x-extent.

Checking that the water collision radius comfortably covers all arm reach points at their extremes, so nothing clips outside the circular footprint — overall the model works out to roughly 11.2 m wide and 5.3 m tall, which seems reasonable but I'm second-guessing whether that's too large overall.

For sizing, fantasy creatures like a kraken warrant this scale given their lore, so an 11 m footprint with a 4.75 m mantle height fits the legendary ship-crusher reputation. I'm now mapping out splash spike placement at radius 2 around the base point, checking they don't collide with arm positions — looks okay. Then I'm planning the mantle's surface detailing by angular zones: dorsal gradient near the top, a dark groove line, a blue gradient flank, a dashed orange accent band, and a cyan belly panel, with glow strips positioned along the flank zone between the other features.

I'm working through the geometry of the glow strips versus the ribs to avoid z-fighting — adjusting strip radius and lift so they sit just under the rib ring height, since the numbers were nearly overlapping. I decide to accept some overlap and treat the ribs as a partial ring rather than a full one to reduce visual conflict.

Writing ring direction function...

Computing a sample table of points and tangents along the mantle curve, then interpolating to find the corresponding y-position for lookups...

Adding chevron and seam patterns...

Setting up arm paint zones with dashed accent lines and seam rings, then starting to write the actual geometry builder code importing the math and path utilities.

Defining interpolation function...

I'm sketching the mantle radius profile as a set of keyframe values forming a teardrop shape, tapering from the base up through a wider bulge and down to a point.

Now I'm writing a band function for generating lathed rings along the mantle, passing the chain point's position and axis to orient each segment.

I'm defining an arm spec type with angle, radius, points, cuffs, and cup data, then building a conversion function that maps angle and lateral offset into world-space coordinates for each arm point.

I'm now building out the chain and sweep logic for each arm, naming the joints sequentially, generating the tentacle mesh along the catmull-rom curve, and adding lathed cuffs at specified points along the chain.

For the suction cups, I'm placing them at alternating angles along the sweep surface using the outward normal direction, spacing nine cups per arm from near the base to near the tip, scaled down relative to the local tentacle radius.

For the tip bead, I'm placing a small glowing sphere just past the end of the chain, letting it inherit position and bone weights from that point so it follows the tentacle's tip naturally, with a minimum radius so it stays visible.

For the beak, I'm sweeping a bezier curve with a radius function that can return either a single value or a width/height pair for an elliptical cross-section, making sure TypeScript correctly infers the tuple type from context rather than widening it to a plain array.

The brows use Catmull-Rom spline through Vector3 points, while the horn sweeps a cubic bezier with a tapering radius from thick base to a near-zero tip, shaded with a gunmetal base transitioning to an orange tip near the end.

For fins, I'm attaching joint bones onto the mantle skeleton near the back, parenting each fin to the appropriate mantle joint with a hinge role so they can swing naturally, then extruding bone geometry from there. Setting up glow strip points...

For the glow strips, I'm sweeping curves along sampled points with the bone set to the whole mantle chain rather than a single joint so they deform with the skinned mesh, while crest blades stay rigid attached to one joint each. Now I'm starting on the head geometry as a sphere primitive.

I'm considering whether to add extra armor plating around the cheeks and jaw, maybe small tooth-like spikes near the mouth, but leaning toward keeping it simpler and skipping the face plate detail.

For richness, I'm weighing additional touches like glowing vein dashes on the mantle, chevron belly paint, eye bezels with brow decals, rib detailing, and a lathe-built shoulder plate ring at the arm roots, while deciding some extras like foam bubble rings aren't necessary.

Deciding to skip the shoulder plate collar idea since the head blob already occupies that space, so I'll move on to writing the final code, including the water surface noise helper and randomized droplet sphere generation around the core.

Adding foam spike rings...

That checks out to about 15 flat colors. Now I'm working out the arm geometry: a tapered radius function shrinking from root to tip, seven joints per arm, with cuff and cup placement values spaced along the limb.

Writing cuff function code...

Confirming the lathe winding matches the cup's orientation, then moving to the jaw joint setup — positioning it at the beak hinge with an aim toward the lower beak, and posing it with a forward rotation to open the mouth. Now I'm adding a second sweep for the lower beak plate structure.

I'm considering a glowing sphere tucked inside the mouth cavity to simulate throat interior, placed between the beaks so it peeks through the small gap when the jaw opens slightly. Then I'm sanity-checking beak proportions against the arm root, and thinking about adding a decorative stripe or chevron detail across the top of the head.

I'm skipping the cheek guard idea and moving to double-check potential runtime issues: making sure the chain/names function signature works correctly, catmull curves accept Vector3 arrays properly, and extrude direction inputs handle Vector3 as expected. Now I'm verifying that the blade outline points don't self-intersect by working out the coordinates carefully.

Setting thickness and bevel values for this part, then checking the fin outline's smoothing — verifying the polygon stays convex so corner-cutting never crosses an edge.

The remaining cross products are all positive too, confirming the shape is convex. Now I'm checking the fin placement relative to the tube radius to make sure it's hidden correctly, then moving on to verify the lathe outline for the water shape is wound counterclockwise.

Checking the water profile points confirm a simple polygon with no self-intersections, and the first/last points sit correctly on the axis.

For the cup outline, I'm tracing through each edge to verify it's also simple and non-intersecting, with the near-axis points staying consistent after scaling. Then I move to the eye sphere with radius 0.4 before continuing to the next check.

Now I'm verifying the `part()` color type accepts a string or Paint fill, and looking into the `glow()` function signature to confirm what target types it accepts before I rely on it.
